claims.source: This indicates that BRAF dimers are not constrained in a symmetrical αC-in/αC-in configuration, as structural models suggest (Park et al., 2019; Liau et al., 2020), but rather that one subunit is free to explore other conformations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from 19F NMR data showing the presence of the dynamic αC-in^broad state.

claims.claim: The binding of a single type II inhibitor molecule can dramatically increase BRAF dimerization because the BRAF dimer only requires one subunit to adopt the locked αC-in conformation.
claims.source: This explains how the binding of a single type II inhibitor molecule, which pays the energetic penalty for locking one BRAF subunit in the αC-in state, can dramatically increase BRAF dimerization, since the BRAF dimer only requires one and not both subunits to adopt the locked αC-in conformation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation that connects the NMR findings with the allosteric coupling results.

claims.claim: The dynamic heterogeneity of the BRAF dimer revealed by NMR may form the foundation for the asymmetric allosteric coupling that gives rise to paradoxical activation of BRAF by type II inhibitors.
claims.source: Thus, the dynamic heterogeneity of the BRAF dimer revealed by NMR may form the foundation for the asymmetric allosteric coupling that gives rise to paradoxical activation of BRAF by type II inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic interpretation connecting NMR data with allosteric coupling and paradoxical activation.

claims.claim: Both FDA-approved αC-out RAF inhibitors and newer αC-in RAF inhibitors trigger paradoxical activation of BRAF.
claims.source: The FDA-approved αC-out RAF inhibitors and the newer αC-in RAF inhibitors currently under development represent fundamentally different classes of drug that have opposite effects on RAF conformation and dimerization. Nonetheless, both drug classes trigger paradoxical activation of BRAF.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of known phenomena.

claims.claim: Activation by αC-out inhibitors is attributed in part to negative allostery.
claims.source: Activation by the αC-out inhibitors is attributed in part to negative allostery, where dimer-disrupting allosteric effects prevent full occupancy of intact dimers (Karoulia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: The model of negative allostery does not provide an adequate explanation for paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors.
claims.source: This model of negative allostery does not provide an adequate explanation for paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors, which are positively coupled to dimerization and have been thought to bind both subunits of the dimer with equal potency (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as motivation for the study.

claims.claim: For type II inhibitors, favorable allostery occurs through an asymmetric coupling mechanism in which the binding of the first inhibitor molecule promotes dimerization much more strongly than binding of the second inhibitor molecule.
claims.source: Remarkably, for type II inhibitors this favorable allostery is not evenly distributed between both binding sites of the dimer, as previously proposed (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), and instead occurs through an asymmetric coupling mechanism in which the binding of the first inhibitor molecule promotes dimerization much more strongly than binding of the second inhibitor molecule.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Allosteric asymmetry triggers selective induction of BRAF dimers with only one subunit bound to inhibitor.
claims.source: We demonstrate that this allosteric asymmetry triggers selective induction of BRAF dimers with only one subunit bound to inhibitor, with larger degrees of asymmetry leading to greater induction of these partially occupied dimers.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The degree of induction of partially occupied dimers fully accounts for both the concentration dependence and amplitude of BRAF activation measured in vitro for 11 different αC-in inhibitors.
claims.source: Indeed, the degree of induction of partially occupied dimers fully accounts for both the concentration dependence and amplitude of BRAF activation measured in vitro for 11 different αC-in inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion, supported by data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Type I inhibitors lack sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through BRAF homodimers.
claims.source: While type II inhibitors are asymmetrically coupled and strongly activate BRAF homodimers, type I inhibitors lack sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through this mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Type I inhibitors induce paradoxical activation through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers.
claims.source: We demonstrate, however, that type I inhibitors induce MAPK pathway activation in melanoma cells, consistent with previous reports (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Heidorn et al., 2010). These observations point to type I inhibitors inducing paradoxical activation through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers, rather than BRAF homodimers, a hypothesis that is consistent with a large body of published work (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Karoulia et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017; Heidorn et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Type I inhibitors bind less tightly to CRAF than BRAF.
claims.source: Because type I inhibitors bind less tightly to CRAF than BRAF, the subunits of a heterodimer will have inherently different drug affinities, providing a window for paradoxical activation in the absence of allosteric asymmetry.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for type I inhibitor activation.

claims.claim: The emergence of clinical resistance to belvarafenib and naporafenib can be mediated by induction of ARAF.
claims.source: In particular, the emergence of clinical resistance to belvarafenib and another type II inhibitor, naporafenib, can be mediated by induction of ARAF (Yen et al., 2021; Tkacik et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Both belvarafenib and naporafenib bind ARAF less potently than BRAF.
claims.source: Since both belvarafenib and naporafenib bind ARAF less potently than BRAF, the disparity in drug affinities for the first and second subunits of ARAF/BRAF heterodimers is likely further boosted over that arising from asymmetric allosteric coupling alone, sustaining activation at higher drug concentrations and conferring resistance.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of resistance mechanisms.

claims.claim: Type I and type II inhibitors stabilize distinct αC-helix conformations in solution.
claims.source: We show that type I and type II inhibitors stabilize distinct αC-helix conformations in solution.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of DEER results.

claims.claim: Type II inhibitors trigger a structural change of the catalytic DFG-motif and activation loop of BRAF that is not accomplished by type I inhibitors.
claims.source: In addition, type II inhibitors trigger a structural change of the catalytic DFG-motif and activation loop of BRAF that is not accomplished by type I inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as known structural information.

claims.claim: The recent cryo-EM structure of dimeric BRAF in complex with 14-3-3 shows an asymmetric arrangement of the BRAF dimer with respect to 14-3-3.
claims.source: The recent cryo-EM structure of dimeric BRAF in complex with the scaffolding protein 14-3-3, determined in the absence of inhibitors, shows an asymmetric arrangement of the BRAF dimer with respect to 14-3-3 (Kondo et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: In the cryo-EM structure, the C-terminal tail of one BRAF subunit binds to and blocks the active site of the opposite subunit, while the reciprocal interaction is prevented.
claims.source: This arrangement permits the C-terminal tail of one subunit to bind to and block the active site of the opposite subunit, while the reciprocal interaction is prevented.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the cryo-EM structure.

claims.claim: Several type II inhibitors including belvarafenib and LY3009120 have entered clinical trials.
claims.source: Several type II inhibitors studied here including belvarafenib (NCT04835805) and LY3009120 (NCT02014116) have entered clinical trials or could be repurposed like the FDA-approved chronic myeloid leukemia drug ponatinib.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as clinical context.

claims.claim: Paradoxical activation by type II inhibitors has been observed in cell lines both with and without elevated RAS activity.
claims.source: However, paradoxical activation by these type II inhibitors has been observed in cell lines both with and without elevated RAS activity (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Karoulia et al., 2016; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2022; Lavoie et al., 2013), and demonstrated to trigger expression of ERK target genes and increased cell proliferation (Lai et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Ponatinib can activate ERK in RAS-mutant cells at concentrations as low as 1 nM.
claims.source: We along with others show that ponatinib can activate ERK in RAS-mutant cells at concentrations as low as 1 nM, and that this activation is only suppressed at concentrations above 1 μM (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), higher than the plasma level achievable in patients (Ye et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Belvarafenib increases MAPK signaling over a concentration range similar to other type II inhibitors like LY3009120.
claims.source: Similarly, while belvarafenib has shown promising activity in preclinical and clinical studies (Yen et al., 2021), it increases MAPK signaling over a concentration range similar to other type II inhibitors like LY3009120, which has shown an unexpected lack of clinical efficacy (Sullivan et al., 2020) despite favorable preclinical results (Peng et al., 2015; Yen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

results.result: Type II RAF inhibitors exhibit asymmetric allosteric coupling to BRAF dimerization, with the first inhibitor binding event (α) contributing orders of magnitude more to dimer stabilization than the second (β), while type I inhibitors show symmetric coupling with comparable α and β values.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C37, C38 are directly supported by global fitting analysis of FRET data shown in Figure 1f,g, demonstrating α values as large as 10^4 and β values no larger than 10^2 for type II inhibitors. Claim C39 shows type I inhibitors have approximately equal α and β values. The experimental design, data quality, and statistical analysis appear robust with well-constrained parameters confirmed by error surface analysis.

results.result: Allosteric asymmetry in type II inhibitors drives selective induction of partially occupied BBD dimers (with one inhibitor bound), with induction amplitude following a hyperbolic relationship with the α/β ratio. Type II inhibitors induce BBD dimers at 11-78% of total BRAF, substantially higher than type I inhibitors (4-11%).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by simulations using parameterized allosteric models (Figure 2a-c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2). The hyperbolic relationship between BBD induction and α/β ratio is demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally (C51, Figure 2c,d). The quantitative predictions from the model are validated against experimental kinase activity data.

results.result: Type II inhibitors induce strong dose-dependent BRAF activation (up to 19-fold) that correlates linearly (R²=0.93) with predicted BBD dimer induction. The catalytic turnover of BBD dimers (3.2±0.3 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) matches published values for fully active BRAF dimers, demonstrating that partially occupied dimers are highly active.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C59 are strongly supported by in vitro kinase activity assays (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2) showing excellent agreement between measured activity and model predictions. The linear correlation (C55, Figure 2e) and turnover calculation (C56-C57) provide quantitative validation. The comparison with published data (Liau et al., 2020) strengthens the conclusion that BBD dimers are catalytically active.

results.result: Type I and type II inhibitors stabilize distinct αC-helix conformations in solution, with type I inhibitor GDC0879 inducing shorter spin-spin distances than type II inhibitors (AZ628, LY3009120, TAK632) in DEER spectroscopy experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by DEER spectroscopy data (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d) showing distinct distance distributions for type I versus type II inhibitors. The experimental approach is appropriate and the data quality appears adequate. However, the structural interpretation could benefit from additional validation, as distance distributions alone provide limited conformational detail.

results.result: Type II inhibitors induce dose-dependent MAPK pathway activation in SK-MEL-2 cells at concentrations below 1 nM, with activation and inhibition occurring at concentrations differing by several orders of magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by flow cytometry data measuring pMEK1/2 and pERK1/2 (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The cellular data show activation at sub-nanomolar concentrations consistent with the ultrapotent binding predicted by the allosteric models. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate controls and replicates (n=3).

results.result: Type I inhibitors induce MAPK pathway activation in SK-MEL-2 cells across a wide concentration range, but this activation is mediated by BRAF:CRAF heterodimers rather than BRAF homodimers, as type I inhibitors lack sufficient allosteric asymmetry and bind CRAF less effectively than BRAF.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is directly supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Claims C67, C93 are inferences supported by the discrepancy between predicted and observed activation windows, combined with cited literature (C68-C70). Claim C71 provides supporting evidence via immunoblot (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The mechanistic interpretation is reasonable but relies partly on inference and prior literature rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: 19F NMR spectroscopy reveals that BRAF homodimers are dynamically asymmetric, with subunits transitioning between a static αC-in state (αC-in^narrow) and a dynamic state with conformational fluctuations (αC-in^broad). The αC-in^broad state shows exchange broadening, concentration-dependent behavior, and temperature-dependent equilibrium with αC-in^narrow.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C81 are well-supported by 19F NMR data (Figure 4a-c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Multiple independent lines of evidence support the two-state dimer model: spectral deconvolution (C75-C76), T2 relaxation (C77), mutation studies (C78), D2O exchange (C79), and temperature dependence (C80-C81). Claims C82-C83 represent reasonable interpretations of the data, though alternative models cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The dynamic asymmetry of BRAF dimers, where only one subunit is locked in the αC-in state, provides a structural mechanism for how binding of a single type II inhibitor molecule can dramatically increase BRAF dimerization and drive paradoxical activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C8 is supported by 19F NMR data (Figure 4). Claims C84-C85 represent mechanistic interpretations connecting the NMR findings with the allosteric coupling data. While the interpretation is logical and consistent with all experimental observations, it remains somewhat speculative as the direct link between dynamic asymmetry and allosteric asymmetry is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. Additional experiments could strengthen this connection.

results.result: Type I inhibitors lack allosteric asymmetry (α ≈ β) and do not activate BRAF homodimers, lacking sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through this mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C92 are supported by allosteric coupling data (Figure 1f,g) showing symmetric α and β values for type I inhibitors. Claim C7 is supported by kinase activity assays (Figure 2) and cellular data (Figure 3) showing minimal activation of BRAF homodimers. The conclusion is well-supported by multiple independent experimental approaches.

results.result: The baseline dimerization affinity of apo BRAF is 62.4±2.9 μM, and all αC-in inhibitors induce large increases in FRET A/D ratio consistent with inhibitor-induced dimerization, with inhibitor-bound BRAF dimerizing with nanomolar affinity.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is directly measured from FRET experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b) and agrees with published values. Claims C35-C36 are supported by FRET data (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The experimental design is appropriate and the measurements appear robust with adequate controls and replicates.

results.result: Type II inhibitors with large α values exhibit picomolar affinity for the first dimer subunit while maintaining substantially weaker affinity for the second subunit, whereas type I inhibitors bind both subunits with comparable affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are calculated from the parameterized allosteric models derived from global fitting of FRET data. The calculations are mathematically sound given the model structure. Independent validation is provided by intramolecular FRET experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 7) and heterodimer experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).

results.result: In BRAF^A481F:BRAF heterodimer experiments that isolate the effects of α, type II inhibitors induce dimerization with low nanomolar affinity (10³-10⁴ fold enhancement), while type I inhibitor GDC0879 fails to induce heterodimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by FRET experiments with BRAF^A481F:BRAF heterodimers (Figure 1—figure supplement 9). This experimental design cleverly isolates the contribution of α by blocking the second binding site. The results are consistent with the asymmetric model for type II inhibitors and symmetric model for type I inhibitors.

results.result: αC-out inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib, encorafenib) disrupt BRAF dimerization, with total decreases in dimerization affinity of 1-2 orders of magnitude, weaker than the dimer promotion by αC-in inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by FRET experiments with BRAF^E586K (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 10) and global fitting analysis (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 6). The use of the E586K mutation to enhance baseline dimerization is appropriate for studying dimer-disrupting inhibitors. The quantitative analysis appears sound.

results.result: Type II RAF inhibitors paradoxically activate BRAF at subsaturating concentrations through induction of BRAF dimers, a phenomenon observed for both FDA-approved αC-out inhibitors and newer αC-in inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C32-C33 represent established knowledge cited from prior literature and confirmed by the current study. Claim C86 summarizes this known phenomenon. While these claims are well-supported by the literature and the current data, they represent background knowledge rather than novel findings of this study.

results.result: For type II inhibitors, favorable allostery occurs through an asymmetric coupling mechanism where the first inhibitor binding event promotes dimerization much more strongly than the second, and this asymmetry fully accounts for the concentration dependence and amplitude of BRAF activation measured in vitro for 11 different αC-in inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C91 represent summary statements of the main findings supported by the comprehensive dataset including FRET experiments (Figure 1), simulations (Figure 2), and kinase activity assays (Figure 2). The quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental measurements across 11 inhibitors provides strong support for the mechanistic model.

results.result: Clinical resistance to belvarafenib and naporafenib can be mediated by induction of ARAF, and since both drugs bind ARAF less potently than BRAF, the disparity in drug affinities for heterodimer subunits may sustain activation at higher drug concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by citations to prior literature. Claim C96 represents a speculative interpretation about resistance mechanisms based on differential binding affinities. While the reasoning is logical, this mechanism is not directly tested in the current study. The claim relies on inference and extrapolation from the BRAF homodimer data to ARAF/BRAF heterodimers.

results.result: Ponatinib activates ERK in RAS-mutant cells at concentrations as low as 1 nM with suppression only above 1 μM (higher than achievable plasma levels), and belvarafenib increases MAPK signaling over a concentration range similar to LY3009120.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by the current flow cytometry data and cited literature (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2017). Claim C104 is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and cited literature. These observations have important clinical implications regarding the therapeutic window for these inhibitors.

results.result: Background on BRAF biology, mutations, and inhibitor development: BRAF is a central MAPK pathway component; V600E is the most prevalent mutation conferring constitutive activity; FDA-approved inhibitors show initial responses but resistance emerges; αC-out inhibitors fail to inhibit dimers due to negative allostery; αC-in inhibitors were developed to bypass this but still cause paradoxical activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C31 represent established background knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout the introduction. These claims provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: Type II inhibitors exhibit asymmetric allosteric coupling with α values as large as 10^4 and β values no larger than 10^2, while type I inhibitors show symmetric coupling with approximately equal α and β values. This asymmetry means binding to the first dimer site dominates the allosteric effect for type II inhibitors.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised this finding. Reviewer 1 called the study 'elegant' with 'compelling and comprehensive evidence' for the allosteric model. Reviewer 2 highlighted the 'beautifully conducted assays' and 'thorough characterization of the allostery.' Reviewer 3 noted the 'distinct patterns' between type I and type II inhibitors and stated the work 'makes a strong case' for the asymmetric coupling mechanism.

results.result: Allosteric asymmetry of type II inhibitors results in efficient and selective induction of partially occupied BBD dimers (one inhibited, one active subunit). The amplitude of BBD induction is primarily dictated by the α/β ratio, with type II inhibitors showing 11-78% BBD induction versus 4-11% for type I inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly stated that 'allosteric asymmetry has the potential for Type II inhibitors to promote dimerization while favoring occupancy of only one subunit (BBD form), leading to the enrichment of an active dimer.' Reviewer 1 noted 'compelling and comprehensive evidence' for the model. No reviewer challenged these simulation-based predictions or the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Type II inhibitors induced strong dose-dependent increases in BRAF kinase activity (up to 19-fold), while type I inhibitors induced only minor increases and αC-out inhibitors showed no activation. There is a linear correlation (R²=0.93) between measured kinase activation and predicted BBD induction, with a catalytic turnover per BBD dimer of 3.2×10⁻³ s⁻¹, matching published values for fully active BRAF dimers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 stated that 'measurements of in vitro BRAF kinase activity correlate amazingly well with the calculated amounts of the half-site-inhibited BBD forms with Type II inhibitors.' Reviewer 1 described the evidence as 'compelling and comprehensive.' The agreement between measured turnover and published values for active dimers was not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: 19F NMR data reveal that BRAF homodimers are dynamically asymmetric, with one subunit locked in the active αC-in state (αC-in^narrow) and the other subunit dynamic (αC-in^broad). This dynamic heterogeneity provides a structural mechanism for how binding of a single αC-in inhibitor molecule can induce potent BRAF dimerization and activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically praised 'the use of F-NMR and DEER spectroscopy' as providing 'important insights into the details of the process.' Reviewer 3 noted that the work 'further show[s] that helix aC adopts multiple states and is therefore dynamic in apo BRAF,' making 'a strong case' for the mechanism. No reviewer questioned the NMR interpretation or the connection to asymmetric coupling.

results.result: DEER spectroscopy experiments show that type I and type II inhibitors induce distinct αC-helix conformations in solution, with type I inhibitor GDC0879 inducing a shorter average spin-spin distance than type II inhibitors AZ628, LY3009120, and TAK632.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly highlighted 'the use of F-NMR and DEER spectroscopy' as providing 'important insights.' Reviewer 3 noted that 'DEER/EPR measurements further examine the positioning of helix aC' and 'show systematic outward movement of aC with Type II inhibitors, relative to the aC-in state with Type I inhibitors.' No concerns were raised about these structural findings.

results.result: Type II inhibitors induced dose-dependent MAPK pathway activation in SK-MEL-2 cells at concentrations below 1 nM, with activation and inhibition occurring at concentrations differing by several orders of magnitude. Type I inhibitors also activated MAPK signaling across a wide concentration range, but this activation is proposed to occur through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers rather than BRAF homodimers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raised a concern: 'it would be helpful to address whether the activation of BRAF by Type II inhibitors, while strongly correlated with BBD model predictions in vitro, also depends on CRAF via BRAF-CRAF in cells and therefore overlaps with the mechanisms of paradoxical activation by Type I and aC-out inhibitors.' This indicates uncertainty about whether type II inhibitor activation in cells is solely through BRAF homodimers or also involves heterodimers.

results.result: Type I inhibitors do not activate BRAF homodimers and lack sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through BRAF homodimers.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted that 'Type I BRAFi binds equally well to the first and second subunits within dimeric BRAF' and that type I inhibitors 'do not fit this model' of homodimer activation. The distinction between type I and type II inhibitors was consistently recognized across all reviews without challenge to this specific claim.

results.result: FRET experiments quantified baseline BRAF dimerization affinity (62.4±2.9 μM), showed that all αC-in inhibitors induced large increases in dimerization with nanomolar affinity at saturating concentrations, and demonstrated that αC-out inhibitors disrupted dimerization with 1-2 orders of magnitude decrease in affinity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 praised the 'beautifully conducted assays that allow for a thorough characterization of the allostery.' Reviewer 3 noted that 'intermolecular FRET measurements quantify Kd for BRAF dimerization and inhibitor binding to the first and second subunits.' No concerns were raised about the FRET methodology or quantitative measurements.

results.result: Type II RAF inhibitors paradoxically activate BRAF at subsaturating concentrations through induction of BRAF dimers, and both FDA-approved αC-out inhibitors and newer αC-in inhibitors trigger paradoxical activation despite having opposite effects on RAF conformation.
results.evaluation: This is established background knowledge that frames the study. Reviewer 1 stated the work presents 'important findings into how small molecules that were originally developed to inhibit the oncogenic kinase, BRAF, instead trigger activation.' All reviewers accepted this as the motivating context without challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the asymmetric allosteric coupling findings for type II inhibitors (C3, C4, C37, C38, C39). OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative FRET data and global fitting analysis, while peer reviewers praised the 'elegant' study with 'compelling and comprehensive evidence.' Peer review also includes C6 (type I inhibitor symmetry) in this evaluation.

Both support the simulation-based predictions about BBD dimer formation and activity (C5, C48-C51, C90). OpenEval highlights the hyperbolic relationship and model validation, while peer reviewers explicitly noted the potential for type II inhibitors to promote dimerization while favoring single-site occupancy. Peer review also includes C89 in this evaluation.

Both strongly support the in vitro kinase activity findings (C52-C59). OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative agreement between measured activity and model predictions, while Reviewer 3 stated the measurements 'correlate amazingly well' with calculated BBD forms. Peer review also includes C91 in this evaluation.

Both support the DEER spectroscopy findings showing distinct conformational states (C60, C61, C97). OpenEval notes the data quality is adequate but structural interpretation could benefit from additional validation. Peer reviewers praised the DEER/EPR measurements showing systematic outward movement of helix αC with type II inhibitors.

Both support the 19F NMR findings about helix αC dynamics and asymmetry (C8, C72-C85). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of multiple lines of evidence supporting the two-state dimer model, while peer reviewers praised the NMR insights and noted the work 'makes a strong case' for the mechanism connecting dynamics to allosteric coupling.

Both address cellular activation by type II inhibitors (C62-C64), but with different emphases. OpenEval supports the claims based on flow cytometry data showing sub-nanomolar activation. Peer review expresses uncertainty (Reviewer 3) about whether cellular activation depends solely on BRAF homodimers or also involves BRAF-CRAF heterodimers, questioning the mechanistic interpretation in cells.

Both address the discrepancy between predicted and observed activation windows and feedback mechanisms (C66-C71, C93). OpenEval notes the mechanistic interpretation relies partly on inference and literature. Peer review raises uncertainty about whether type II inhibitor activation overlaps with paradoxical activation mechanisms involving CRAF.

Both support that type I inhibitors show symmetric binding and minimal BRAF homodimer activation (C6, C7, C92). OpenEval cites multiple experimental approaches, while peer reviewers noted type I inhibitors 'do not fit this model' of homodimer activation and bind equally well to both subunits.

Both support the basic FRET measurements of dimerization and binding (C34-C36). OpenEval emphasizes the agreement with published values and robust experimental design. Peer review (R8) groups these with additional FRET experiments (C43-C47) and praises the 'beautifully conducted assays.'

OpenEval supports the calculated binding parameters from allosteric models (C41-C42) with validation from intramolecular FRET and heterodimer experiments. Peer review R8 addresses overlapping FRET methodology but focuses on different specific claims (C34-C36, C43-C47), praising the thorough characterization of allostery.

Both support the heterodimer FRET experiments isolating α contribution (C43-C45). OpenEval praises the clever experimental design blocking the second binding site. Peer review R8 groups these with other FRET measurements and notes the quantification of binding to first and second subunits.

OpenEval supports the E586K mutation experiments for studying dimer-disrupting inhibitors (C46-C47). Peer review R8 includes these claims within broader praise for FRET methodology but does not specifically comment on the E586K experiments.

Both support the background knowledge about paradoxical activation and type I inhibitor effects (C1, C2, C32, C33, C86). OpenEval notes these represent established knowledge rather than novel findings. Peer reviewers accepted this as motivating context without challenge.

Both address the connection between NMR dynamics and allosteric coupling (C8, C84, C85). OpenEval notes the interpretation is logical but somewhat speculative as the direct link is inferred. Peer review R4 encompasses broader NMR findings (C72-C85) and supports the mechanistic connection without expressing reservations.

Both address summary statements about asymmetric coupling mechanisms (C89, C91). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative agreement across 11 inhibitors. Peer review R2 focuses on the BBD formation predictions (C89 included), while R3 addresses the kinase activity correlation (C91 included).

OpenEval evaluates claims about resistance mechanisms and differential binding to ARAF/BRAF heterodimers (C95, C96) as UNCERTAIN, noting the mechanism is not directly tested and relies on inference. No corresponding peer review evaluation was found for these specific resistance mechanism claims.

OpenEval supports claims about therapeutic window implications and paradoxical activation at higher concentrations (C103, C104) based on flow cytometry data and literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these therapeutic window claims.

OpenEval evaluates extensive background knowledge claims from the introduction (C10-C31) as appropriately cited established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific background claims, as peer reviewers focused on novel findings rather than cataloging introduction content.
